summary: Defines common semantics and data formats for presence so gateways can connect different presence services. When it was written, many instant messaging systems used incompatible protocols, with little interoperability between them.

eli5.summary: Different chat apps spoke different languages. This document makes a common way to say who is online so translators can connect them.

questions: presence interoperability between instant messaging services
what is the common profile for presence
what is the pres uri scheme
how do you unsubscribe from presence
subtitle: A shared abstract model of presence so gateways can link instant messaging services that speak different protocols.

tldr.problem: Many presence protocols, mostly parts of commercial instant messaging services, were in use and little interoperability between them had been achieved.
tldr.mechanism: CPP defines three abstract operations (subscribe, response and notify), a pres: URI scheme and a requirement to carry presence in the PIDF format, so that gateways can map between services.
tldr.outcome: A presence protocol that supports all the operations can connect to a CPP gateway. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no replacement.

facts.label: TransID and SubscriptID length
facts.value: Gateways should handle up to 40 bytes

today: RFC 3859 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It relies on RFC 3863 for the presence document format and on RFC 2778 for the presence model.

sections.title: Why a Common Profile
sections.content:
Presence is defined in RFC 2778. When RFC 3859 was written, numerous presence protocols were in use, largely as components of commercial instant messaging services, and little interoperability between services based on them had been achieved. The Common Profile for Presence (CPP) defines semantics and data formats for the common presence services so that gateways between presence services can be built.

Service behavior is described abstractly, as operations invoked between the consumer and the provider of a service. Each presence service must say how that behavior maps onto its own protocol. The strategy is a local matter, as long as there is a clear relation between the abstract behavior and how a particular service faithfully realizes it. One service might send key/value pairs, another a compact binary form, a third nested containers.
sections.eli5: Every chat app talks in its own way. This document writes down a simple shared list of questions and answers, and each app decides how to say them in its own language.

sections.title: Gateways and Presence Services
sections.content:
CPP reuses the vocabulary of RFC 2778, such as PRESENCE, OPEN, CLOSED and INSTANT INBOX. It adds the term CPP gateway: a network element that interworks between diverse presence protocols, relaying a common payload. The RFC admits that calling these elements gateways or relays is somewhat debatable.

A client that sends an operation to a presence service might reach an endpoint or an intermediary such as a CPP gateway. The client should not have to know which, because responses from either look the same.

To interface with a gateway, a protocol must support all the operations in the document, meaning it has some message or capability providing each function. The attributes are only the minimum needed for interoperability. A protocol may carry additional information that CPP does not map.
sections.eli5: A gateway is a translator standing between two chat apps. The app asking questions should not need to know whether it is talking to the real thing or the translator.

sections.title: The Subscribe, Response and Notify Operations
sections.content:
An application that wants a PRESENTITY's presence information invokes subscribe. Its attributes are watcher, target, duration, SubscriptID and TransID. The duration is the maximum number of seconds the subscription should be active. A duration of zero means a one-time request for the current presence information. Gateways should be able to handle TransIDs and SubscriptIDs up to 40 bytes long.

The service immediately answers with response, carrying status, the same TransID and a duration, which may differ from the one requested. On success the service immediately invokes notify, whose content is the presence information. For the rest of a non-zero duration it invokes notify again whenever the presence information changes. The application does not answer a notify.

CPP assumes the presence protocols below it deliver messages reliably, and adds no application-layer delivery assurance.
sections.eli5: You ask a friend to tell you whenever someone's status changes. They say yes right away, tell you the current status, and then keep telling you about changes until the time you asked for runs out.

sections.title: How a Service Handles Subscribe
sections.content:
When the service is told of a subscribe, it checks in order:

  • If the watcher or target does not refer to a valid PRESENTITY, it invokes a response with status failure.
  • If access control does not permit the request, the response is again failure.
  • If the duration is non-zero and the watcher and target match an in-progress subscribe for the application, the response is failure.
  • Otherwise, if the service can deliver, it sends a success response and an immediate notify, then further notifies on changes while access control allows.

A service must keep presence information and continuing operations such as periodic notification in persistent storage. Because a SubscriptID is long-lived, the values generated should be unique across a significant duration of time, and intrinsically globally unique, not just unique for one watcher and presentity pair.
sections.eli5: The service first checks that the people exist, that you are allowed to ask and that you are not already asking. If all is well it says yes and starts sending updates.

sections.title: Cancelling and Polling with Zero Duration
sections.content:
There is no separate unsubscribe or fetch operation. To end a subscription, the application invokes subscribe with a duration of 0 and the SubscriptID of the existing subscription. A notify is still invoked when a subscription is cancelled this way, and the watcher can discard it.

To get presence information once without starting a lasting subscription, the application sends subscribe with a duration of 0 and a new SubscriptID. In both cases the service responds immediately with the matching TransID.
sections.eli5: Saying 'tell me for zero minutes' with a new ticket gets you one answer now. Saying it with an old ticket cancels that old request.

sections.title: Presence URIs and Address Resolution
sections.content:
A PRESENTITY is named with the PRES URI scheme, for example pres:fred@example.com. A WATCHER identifies itself the same way. The syntax follows the mailto: URI: pres:, an optional mailbox, and optional ? headers. Using a pres: URI is meant to start the user's instant messaging application with the address and headers filled in.

To find the next hop for an operation, a client resolves the domain name part of the destination. Implementations SHOULD follow the guidelines for dereferencing URIs in RFC 3861.

An appendix notes that mappings placing special information in the im: local part MUST use the meta-syntax of RFC 2846. It also describes a source-routing style mapping, which it says is usually least friendly to humans, so software should perform it automatically.
sections.eli5: A pres address looks like an email address, such as fred at example.com, so everyone knows who is being asked about.

sections.title: Presence Information Format
sections.content:
CPP defines semantics, not syntax, for notifications. But some properties, especially security, only work end to end if the interoperating protocols share a common format. So applications that send notifications through a CPP gateway MUST support the PIDF format of RFC 3863. They MAY support other formats.

CPP gateways MUST be able to relay the body of a notification between supported presence protocols without modifying or inspecting it.
sections.eli5: Everyone agrees to write the status on the same kind of card, and the translator passes the card along without opening it.

sections.title: Security and Gateways
sections.content:
Detailed security considerations come from RFC 2779. CPP gateways MUST meet the minimum security requirements of the presence protocols they connect. Gateways add new risks: confidentiality and integrity between presentities and watchers can only be end to end if the protocols share a common presence format.

When end-to-end security is required, notify MUST use PIDF and MUST protect the PIDF MIME body with S/MIME, using encryption and/or signatures. AES should be preferred, though only the baseline S/MIME and CMS algorithms are required. Certificates used for S/MIME presence SHOULD carry the subject's PRES URI in a subjectAltName field, and widely accepted trust anchors are encouraged. Anonymous presence is out of scope.
sections.eli5: If a secret message passes through a translator, it should be locked in an envelope only the receiver can open, so the translator cannot peek or change it.
